notes:
I've written notes for most verses in Acts 13:27–52, but some have only thin coverage. My searches cut off before I could read the full Enduring Word (Guzik) commentary for this part of the chapter or the full Precept Austin page. Points from those two sites come from search-result summaries, not full readings.

The one verse where Protestant traditions clearly disagree is **v. 48** ("appointed for eternal life"). There is also a real split over what "today I have begotten you" means in **v. 33**. I found nothing from the Catholic, Orthodox, modern-scholarship (bibleodyssey, NET notes) or prosperity/word-of-faith/hyper-grace sites on this passage, so those are left out. Where a page names a commentator's tradition, I give it; otherwise I don't.

---

**vv. 27–29**
- Guzik groups vv. 24–29 as Paul showing how people both received and rejected Jesus, with John the Baptist as the example of receiving Him. https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/acts-13/
- On "the tree" (v. 29), the French edition of Guzik says the background is the law that a person hanged on a tree is cursed by God. Paul's point is that Jesus was cursed so we could be blessed (Galatians 3:13). https://fr.enduringword.com/actes-13/
- Precept Austin (on vv. 27ff) describes the rulers as people who read the Prophets, but they didn't allow the Prophets to read them. https://www.preceptaustin.org/acts-13-commentary

**vv. 30–31**
- Guzik stresses "But God": people did their worst against God, but He was greater, and Jesus rose victorious over sin and death. https://fr.enduringword.com/actes-13/
- Guzik also notes that Paul's preaching was about events, things that really happened, not philosophy. https://fr.enduringword.com/actes-13/
- Chuck Smith calls the resurrection the heart of the gospel, in fact, without the resurrection, you have no gospel. https://www.blueletterbible.org/Comm/smith_chuck/SermonNotes_Act/Act_107.cfm

**vv. 32–33**
- Guzik: the resurrection shows Jesus is truly the unique Son of God (Psalm 2:7). https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/acts-13/
- Barnes says the resurrection completed or perfected the fulfillment of the promises; he does not claim every part of the promise was about the resurrection. https://biblehub.com/commentaries/acts/13-33.htm
- **Where interpreters differ: what "today I have begotten You" refers to**
  - Barnes: Paul's use here settles that the Psalm is not about eternal generation or the incarnation. Jesus is called Son here because God raised Him. https://biblehub.com/commentaries/acts/13-33.htm
  - Matthew Henry: the words can describe Christ's eternal generation. They apply to the resurrection only in a secondary sense, meaning it made His sonship visible. https://www.blueletterbible.org/Comm/mhc/Act/Act_013.cfm
  - Gill accepts a resurrection reference, but without any detriment to the doctrine of Christ's eternal generation and sonship. https://www.studylight.org/bible/lat/nvl/acts/13-33.html
  - Clarke (Wesleyan) records that it has long been disputed whether the verse means the incarnation or the resurrection. https://www.studylight.org/commentary/acts/13-33.html
  - Sam Storms (charismatic): the "day" of begetting was the day of his resurrection and exaltation, and he treats Acts 13:32–33 as the key to reading the Psalm. https://www.samstorms.org/enjoying-god-blog/post/-you-are-my-son-today-i-have-begotten-you
  - Chuck Smith: the phrase can mean either the incarnation or the resurrection, but Paul applies it to the resurrection. https://www.blueletterbible.org/Comm/smith_chuck/SermonNotes_Act/Act_107.cfm

**v. 34**
- Chuck Smith says this quotes Isaiah 55:3, God's promise to David that one of his descendants would always sit on the throne. https://www.blueletterbible.org/Comm/smith_chuck/SermonNotes_Act/Act_107.cfm
- Biblehub's study note: the resurrection made Jesus the promised King from David's line. https://biblehub.com/acts/13-33.htm

**vv. 35–37**
- Precept Austin identifies v. 35 as Paul quoting the messianic Psalm 16:10. https://www.preceptaustin.org/acts-13-commentary
- Guzik: Psalm 16:10 shows Jesus was completely holy even in His work on the cross. https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/acts-13/
- Smith's commentary: David could not have been speaking about himself, because his own body decayed; Jesus' did not. https://www.studylight.org/commentary/acts/13-33.html
- Matthew Henry (on v. 36): each of us should serve our own generation, but Christ was to serve every generation. https://biblehub.com/commentaries/acts/13-33.htm

**vv. 38–39**
- Guzik: forgiveness cancels our debt of sin, while justification puts a positive credit on our account before God. https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/acts-13/
- Ellicott calls v. 39 the seed of Paul's later teaching, and notes that "in Him" points to Christ as the place where forgiveness is found. https://biblehub.com/commentaries/acts/13-39.htm
- Barnes: the Law's sacrifices only pictured a greater sacrifice and could not take sin away. Revealing a way of pardon was left for the gospel. https://biblehub.com/commentaries/acts/13-39.htm
- Gill (Baptist): the law cannot justify, because our obedience is imperfect, so the law curses and condemns. https://www.studylight.org/bible/eng/kjv/acts/13-39.html
- **Where interpreters differ: does the law justify from *some* sins?**
  - A sermon outline on Biblehub says Moses justified from some sins, but faith in Christ justifies from all. https://biblehub.com/sermons/acts/13-39.htm
  - Coffman (Restoration Movement) rejects that reading. In his view "all things" fail to be justified under the law. https://www.studylight.org/commentary/acts/13-39.html
  - Jamieson-Fausset-Brown agrees with Coffman: the "from which" clause explains the main statement rather than making an exception. https://biblehub.com/commentaries/acts/13-39.htm

**vv. 40–41**
- Guzik: Paul quotes Habakkuk about judgment on Jerusalem. Anyone who does not embrace Jesus with their whole life is a "despiser" who will perish. https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/acts-13/
- Precept Austin: the Babylonians brought judgment in time, but rejecting the Messiah brings eternal judgment. https://www.preceptaustin.org/acts-13-commentary
- Guzik also answers critics who say Paul preached too much like Peter: it shows they preached the same gospel. https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/acts-13/

**vv. 42–43**
- Guzik's text (NKJV) says it was the Gentiles who begged to hear more. https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/acts-13/
- Matthew Henry: the hearers could not grasp or remember everything at first hearing, so they asked for it again. Being urged to "continue" in grace implies they had already accepted it. https://www.blueletterbible.org/Comm/mhc/Act/Act_013.cfm

**vv. 44–45**
- Guzik: what drew the crowds was mainly the power of the word of God, not novelty. https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/acts-13/
- Guzik: the leaders' envy is what happens to people more concerned with popularity than with serving God. They also wanted to keep Jews and Gentiles separate. https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/acts-13/

**vv. 46–47**
- Precept Austin: their boldness shows Paul and Barnabas were filled with the Spirit. The Jews were really rejecting the gospel, and God Himself, not the two men. https://www.preceptaustin.org/acts-13-commentary
- Matthew Henry: those who push the gospel away have it justly taken from them, and so they judge themselves unworthy of eternal life. https://www.blueletterbible.org/Comm/mhc/Act/Act_013.cfm
- Guzik: Paul wisely moved to more open hearts, yet he kept praying for Israel (Romans 10:1). https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/acts-13/

**v. 48: the main disagreement between traditions**
- *Reformed and Calvinist readings*
  - Pulpit Commentary: the phrase can only refer to the predestination or election of God, which is what moved them to believe. https://biblehub.com/commentaries/acts/13-48.htm
  - Jamieson-Fausset-Brown: God's ordaining to life is the cause of faith, not its effect. https://biblehub.com/commentaries/acts/13-48.htm
  - Geneva note: since not everyone believed, some must have been ordained, and God's appointing causes faith, not the other way round. https://biblehub.com/commentaries/acts/13-48.htm
  - Gill (Baptist, Calvinist): faith is the fruit of an eternal, unconditional election. He rejects the translation "disposed," saying the ancient versions don't support it. https://www.studylight.org/commentary/acts/13-48.html
  - Calvin: the ordained are those grafted into Christ by faith. https://www.studylight.org/commentary/acts/13-48.html
  - Barnes (Presbyterian) is more qualified. He says the verse is not directly about an eternal decree but about people then inclined to embrace life, a disposition that came from God, not from themselves. https://www.studylight.org/bible/lat/cvl/acts/13-48.html
- *Wesleyan and Arminian readings*
  - Adam Clarke says the text has been most pitifully misunderstood. The Greek word carries no idea of "pre-ordination," and not everyone who believed that day necessarily persevered. https://www.studylight.org/commentary/acts/13-48.html
  - John Wesley, as quoted in the People's New Testament, says the word is never used in Scripture for eternal predestination; those "now ordained" are those who "now believed." https://www.studylight.org/bible/eng/nas/acts/13-48.html
  - Benson argues that if the decree decides who believes, then the lack of a decree decides who doesn't. https://biblehub.com/commentaries/acts/13-48.htm
  - Coffman and Gann (Restoration Movement, Arminian): God ordained beforehand that whoever hears and submits will receive life. https://www.studylight.org/commentary/acts/13-48.html
- *Middle positions*
  - Ellicott prefers "disposed for." He suggests the King James translators may have chosen "ordained" because of the Calvinist leanings of the English Church at the time. https://biblehub.com/commentaries/acts/13-48.htm
  - The Expositor's Greek Testament mentions reading the verb as "had set themselves," the opposite of the Jews judging themselves unworthy in v. 46. https://biblehub.com/commentaries/acts/13-48.htm
  - Bengel: Luke, writing history, points to grace working through the gospel at that moment, which comes from election. https://biblehub.com/commentaries/acts/13-48.htm
  - Matthew Henry gives both readings. https://www.studylight.org/commentary/acts/13-48.html
- *Other notes on v. 48*
  - Chuck Smith simply ties the verse to predestination. https://www.studylight.org/commentary/acts/13-48.html
  - Ellicott on the rejoicing: The joy was not an evanescent burst of emotion. https://biblehub.com/acts/13-48.htm

**v. 49**
- Matthew Henry: the further the word of the Lord spreads, the brighter it shines, like the sun rather than a candle. He also says city believers should take it to ordinary country people. https://www.blueletterbible.org/Comm/mhc/Act/Act_013.cfm
- Precept Austin traces "the word of God/the Lord" through vv. 44–49 as Luke's theme. https://www.preceptaustin.org/acts-13-commentary

**v. 50**
- The Biblical Illustrator explains the women as "devout" in the sense of converts to Judaism and "honourable" in social rank; the persecutors used their influence. https://www.studylight.org/commentary/acts/13-52.html
- Guzik: wherever there is revival, the devil is the second one stirred up. https://fr.enduringword.com/actes-13/
- Matthew Henry: Satan is most enraged when preachers succeed. https://www.blueletterbible.org/Comm/mhc/Act/Act_013.cfm

**v. 51**
- Ellicott: this was literal obedience to Jesus' command (Matthew 10:14). It declared that the unbelieving Jews, not the heathen, were the ones making the ground unclean. https://biblehub.com/acts/13-51.htm
- Clarke: Jews returning from heathen lands shook off foreign dust at the border. https://www.studylight.org/commentary/acts/13-51.html
- Calvin: the act was a sign of cursing, showing how serious contempt for God's word is. https://www.studylight.org/commentary/acts/13-51.html
- Got Questions compares it to "I wash my hands of it": the messengers had done all they could. https://www.gotquestions.org/shake-dust-off-feet.html

**v. 52**
- Guzik: being filled with joy and being filled with the Holy Spirit go together, and their joy was the opposite of what their circumstances would suggest. https://fr.enduringword.com/actes-13/
- William Kelly: God turns the enemy's wickedness into a blessing for His own people. https://www.studylight.org/commentary/acts/13-51.html
- Matthew Henry (via Biblehub): the more our hearts are full of these comforts, the better prepared we are to face hardship. https://biblehub.com/commentaries/acts/13-51.htm
